title: The Ranking That Changed the Club
passage:
A large high school introduced an online system that displayed participation points for extracurricular clubs. Students received points for attending practices, joining events, and completing assigned tasks. The original purpose was modest: club advisers wanted a convenient record because paper attendance sheets were often incomplete. A software update added a public ranking showing the highest point totals. Almost immediately, behavior changed. Some students found the ranking motivating and attended more regularly. Club leaders liked being able to recognize members who contributed often. Yet problems appeared within weeks. In the volunteer club, students began choosing short activities that earned points instead of less visible tasks such as preparing materials or training younger members. In the music club, an injured student continued attending practice even when rest would have been wiser because she feared falling in the ranking. Some members who joined late in the year believed they could never catch up and stopped paying attention to the system entirely. The student council reviewed the issue. At first, members proposed improving the formula by giving more points to difficult tasks. However, advisers warned that difficulty was hard to compare across clubs. Was one hour organizing equipment more valuable than one hour helping a beginner? Should a performance count more than rehearsal? Every adjustment would express a judgment about what kinds of contribution mattered. The council then noticed a deeper issue: the system had changed from a record into a target. When points were private, they described participation imperfectly. Once the ranking became public, students started making choices in order to improve the number itself. The number no longer measured the same behavior it had measured before. A teacher introduced the council to a general idea: when a measure becomes a strong target, people may optimize the measure rather than the underlying goal. The students found examples outside school. A store judged only by the number of customers served might rush each customer. A class judged only by average test scores might avoid difficult material. The council did not conclude that measurement was useless. Without records, advisers had relied on memory, which could also be unfair. Instead, they redesigned the system. Attendance records remained, but the public ranking disappeared. Clubs could choose several private indicators relevant to their own goals, and advisers were encouraged to discuss contributions that numbers missed. The volunteer club tracked both event participation and preparation work. The music club recorded attendance but treated health-related absence separately. Students could view their own history without being placed in a single schoolwide order. Several months later, participation did not collapse as some had predicted. Some students missed the competitive ranking, but many reported less pressure to collect points. The council also found that conversations about contribution became more detailed because leaders had to explain why a task mattered instead of pointing to one score. Hana, who led the review, came away with a complicated view of data. She still believed measurements could reveal patterns and reduce vague judgments. But she no longer assumed that a measurement system simply observes behavior from outside. Once people know how they are being measured, the system can enter the situation and change what they do. That means designers must ask not only whether a metric is accurate, but also what behavior it may encourage, what it leaves invisible, and whether people can improve the score without improving the real thing the score was meant to represent.

The council later tested whether private personal dashboards created similar pressure even without a public ranking. Some students still focused heavily on their totals, while others barely looked at them. This showed that privacy reduced comparison but did not completely remove the influence of measurement. Advisers began using the dashboard as a conversation starter rather than a judgment. A low number could lead to questions about illness, work, transportation, or whether a student had contributed in ways the system did not record. A high number did not automatically prove leadership or quality. The council also set a schedule to review each metric at the end of the year. If a measure produced unwanted behavior or no longer matched a club's goals, it could be changed or removed. Hana liked this rule because measurement systems often become permanent simply because they already exist. Treating metrics as tools that require maintenance made the school more cautious about adding new ones. The final policy stated that important decisions such as awards or leadership selection should not depend on one score alone.
translation:
ある高校では部活動への参加を記録するオンライン制度を導入しました。練習参加、行事、担当作業などでポイントが付き、当初の目的は紙の出席表より正確に記録することでした。しかし更新でポイント上位者の公開ランキングが加わると、行動そのものが変わりました。参加が増えた生徒もいましたが、ボランティア部では地味な準備や後輩指導より短時間で点になる活動を選ぶ人が増え、音楽部ではけがをした生徒が順位を落としたくないため休まず参加する問題も起きました。年度途中に入部した生徒は追いつけないと感じ、制度自体を無視するようになりました。生徒会は難しい作業の点を増やす案を考えましたが、部活ごとに作業の難しさや価値を公平に比べることは困難でした。ここで、制度が『記録』から『目標』に変わったことが重要だと分かりました。非公開のときポイントは不完全ながら参加を表していましたが、順位が目標になると、生徒は本当の活動より数字を増やすよう行動を変え、数字が以前と同じものを測らなくなったのです。先生から『指標が強い目標になると、人は本来の目的ではなく指標そのものを最適化することがある』という考えを教わり、生徒たちは、客数だけで評価される店が接客を急いだり、平均点だけで評価される授業が難しい内容を避けたりする例を考えました。ただし測定自体を廃止したわけではありません。記録がなければ顧問の記憶に頼り、それも不公平になり得ます。そこで出席記録は残し、公開順位は廃止し、部ごとに目的に合う複数指標を非公開で使い、数字に表れない貢献も話し合う方式にしました。参加率は大きく落ちず、点集めの圧力が減ったという声が増えました。レビューを担当した花は、データはパターンを示し曖昧な判断を減らせる一方、測定制度は外から行動を見るだけではなく、人が測られ方を知ると行動そのものを変えると学びました。指標を作るときは、正確さだけでなく、何を促し、何を見えなくし、本来の目的を改善せず数字だけ改善できないかまで考える必要があるのです。

生徒会は、公開順位をなくしても個人用ダッシュボードが同じような圧力を生むか調べました。合計点を強く気にする生徒もいれば、ほとんど見ない生徒もいました。非公開にすれば比較は減りますが、測定そのものの影響が完全になくなるわけではありません。顧問は数値を判定ではなく会話のきっかけとして使い、低い数字なら病気、仕事、交通事情、記録されない貢献などを確認しました。高い数字も自動的にリーダーシップや質を証明するものではありません。各指標は年度末に見直し、望ましくない行動を生んだり目的に合わなくなったりすれば変更・削除することにしました。花は、指標も維持管理が必要な道具として扱うことで、新しい数字を安易に増やさなくなると考えました。表彰や役職選びなど重要な決定は一つの点数だけに依存しない方針になりました。
